description: Microchip/Atmel AT24C256C 256-Kbit (32,768 x 8 bytes) serial EEPROM with an I2C interface: 64-byte page writes, 5 ms self-timed write cycle, 1,000,000 write cycles, 40-year data retention. Runs on 1.7-5.5 V. Sold as: YL-90 AT24C256 I2C EEPROM module (red board, 4-pin header VCC, GND, SCL, SDA, 10 kOhm pull-ups on SDA/SCL), I2C address 0x50.

buildNotes: Address 0x50: the YL-90 module ties A0-A2 low (the chip also pulls floating address pins low). Other modules with A0/A1/A2 jumpers give 0x50-0x57.

Each write uses two address bytes (high byte first) and may hold at most one 64-byte page: bytes past the page end wrap to the START of the same page and overwrite it. The driver splits writes at page boundaries.
After every write the chip is busy for up to 5 ms (tWR) and does not acknowledge its address; the driver waits and then polls for the ACK.
WP must be low (it is on the YL-90) for writes to work; with WP at VCC the whole array is read-only.
Endurance is about 1,000,000 writes per byte: never write in a fast loop, only when a value actually changes.

driver.code:
# AT24C256 256-Kbit (32,768 x 8) I2C serial EEPROM, MicroPython driver.
# Written from the Microchip/Atmel AT24C256C datasheet (Atmel-8568F):
# - device address 1010 A2 A1 A0 (0x50-0x57; 0x50 with A2..A0 at GND)
# - two word-address bytes (high byte first; bit 15 is don't-care, 15 bits used)
# - 64-byte pages: during a write the low 6 address bits wrap inside the page,
#   so writes are split at page boundaries here
# - self-timed write cycle tWR = 5 ms max; the chip NACKs its address until done
#   (acknowledge polling)
# - random read = dummy write of the address, repeated start, then sequential read
import time

SIZE = 32768
PAGE = 64
T_WR_MS = 5


class AT24C256:
    def __init__(self, i2c, addr=0x50):
        self.i2c = i2c
        self.addr = addr

    def _check(self, mem, n):
        if mem < 0 or n < 0 or mem + n > SIZE:
            raise ValueError("address out of range")

    def _wait_ready(self, timeout_ms=20):
        # Acknowledge polling: the EEPROM only ACKs its address once the
        # internal write cycle has finished.
        time.sleep_ms(T_WR_MS)
        t0 = time.ticks_ms()
        while True:
            try:
                self.i2c.writeto(self.addr, b"")
                return
            except OSError:
                if time.ticks_diff(time.ticks_ms(), t0) > timeout_ms:
                    raise OSError("AT24C256 busy (no ACK after write)")
                time.sleep_ms(1)

    def read(self, mem, n):
        """Read n bytes starting at address mem (sequential read)."""
        self._check(mem, n)
        self.i2c.writeto(self.addr, bytes([(mem >> 8) & 0x7F, mem & 0xFF]), False)
        return self.i2c.readfrom(self.addr, n)

    def write(self, mem, data):
        """Write bytes at address mem, split into page writes of at most 64 bytes."""
        data = bytes(data)
        self._check(mem, len(data))
        i = 0
        while i < len(data):
            room = PAGE - (mem % PAGE)  # bytes left in this page
            chunk = data[i:i + room]
            self.i2c.writeto(self.addr, bytes([(mem >> 8) & 0x7F, mem & 0xFF]) + chunk)
            self._wait_ready()
            mem += len(chunk)
            i += len(chunk)

    def read_byte(self, mem):
        return self.read(mem, 1)[0]

    def write_byte(self, mem, value):
        self.write(mem, bytes([value & 0xFF]))

example.code:
from machine import I2C, Pin
import time
from at24c256 import AT24C256

i2c = I2C({I2C_ID}, sda=Pin({SDA}), scl=Pin({SCL}))
ee = AT24C256(i2c)
msg = b'Hello EEPROM'
ee.write(0x003A, msg)  # crosses the 64-byte page boundary at 0x0040; the driver splits it
while True:
    print('EEPROM: ' + ee.read(0x003A, len(msg)).decode())
    time.sleep(1)

# AT24C256 I2C EEPROM module (AT24C256)

## Overview
The **AT24C256C** (Microchip, formerly Atmel) is a 256-Kbit serial EEPROM: 32,768 bytes, organised as 512 pages of 64 bytes, that keep their contents with the power off (40-year retention, 1,000,000 write cycles). It talks I2C. Hobbyists buy it on the red **YL-90 AT24C256 module**: the chip, two 10 kΩ pull-ups on SDA/SCL, A0–A2 and WP tied low, and a 4-pin header.

## Pinout (YL-90 module, header order)
| Pin | Function |
|---|---|
| VCC | Supply, 1.7–5.5 V (3.3 V with an ESP32/Pico) |
| GND | Ground |
| SCL | I2C clock (10 kΩ pull-up on board) |
| SDA | I2C data (10 kΩ pull-up on board) |

## Electrical limits
- Supply: 1.7–5.5 V; no regulator on the module, so VCC is the I2C logic level too.
- Current: about 1 mA reading, 2–3 mA during a write, a few µA standby.
- I2C up to 400 kHz at 1.7 V, 1 MHz at 2.5 V and above.

## Interface details
- **I2C address 0x50** (1010 A2 A1 A0; 0x50–0x57 on boards with address jumpers).
- Every access starts with **two word-address bytes**, high byte first (bit 15 is don't-care).
- **Write**: address bytes + 1…64 data bytes, then STOP. Only the low 6 address bits count up during a write: bytes past the end of a 64-byte page **wrap to the start of the same page** and overwrite it. Split writes at page boundaries.
- **Write cycle**: after STOP the chip is busy for up to **5 ms** (tWR) and NACKs its address; poll for the ACK before the next access.
- **Read**: write the two address bytes (no STOP), repeated START, read as many bytes as you like; the address rolls over from 0x7FFF to 0x0000.
- WP high = whole array read-only; WP low (YL-90) = writes allowed.

## Wiring
- ESP32: VCC → 3V3, GND → GND, SDA → D21, SCL → D22.
- Pico: VCC → 3V3(OUT), GND → GND, SDA → GP4, SCL → GP5.
- Raspberry Pi 4: VCC → pin 1 (3.3 V), GND → pin 6, SDA → pin 3, SCL → pin 5.

## Using the driver
```python
from machine import I2C, Pin
from at24c256 import AT24C256
i2c = I2C(0, sda=Pin(21), scl=Pin(22))
ee = AT24C256(i2c)            # addr=0x50
ee.write(0x0000, b'hello')    # split into page writes, waits out tWR
print(ee.read(0x0000, 5))     # b'hello'
```

## Gotchas
- The datasheet does not promise what a new chip contains (usually 0xFF): store a marker or checksum with your settings and fall back to defaults when it is missing.
- Writing more than one page in a single transfer silently overwrites the start of the page: always use the driver's `write`, which splits at 64-byte boundaries.
- Endurance is about 1,000,000 writes per byte: write only when a value changes, never every loop.
- `OSError` right after a write means the write cycle was not over yet; wait 5 ms or poll for the ACK.
- Do not power it from 5 V when SDA/SCL go to a 3.3 V board: the module's pull-ups go to VCC.
